title: When would you choose Redis Sentinel versus Redis Cluster — Sentinel for lightweight data (sessions, OTPs, tokens) needing automatic master failover via quorum, Cluster for large/high-QPS caches needing horizontal scaling (data sharded across 16384 hash slots by `CRC16(key) % 16384`, each master with replicas), and why is the first question "what kind of data is in Redis?"
shortTitle: When would you choose Redis Sentinel versus Redis Cluster?

s1_definition.profdef: Redis Sentinel and Redis Cluster solve two different problems. Sentinel provides high availability for a single logical dataset that fits on one node: a set of Sentinel processes monitor one master and its replicas, and when a quorum of Sentinels agrees the master is down, they promote a replica and update clients, giving automatic failover without sharding. Redis Cluster provides horizontal scaling and high availability together by partitioning the keyspace across 16384 hash slots, assigning ranges of slots to multiple masters (each with its own replicas), and routing every key to its slot with the formula CRC16 of the key modulo 16384, so the data and the request load spread across many nodes. The reason the first question is always "what kind of data is in Redis?" is that the answer tells you whether the dataset fits on one node and needs only failover (Sentinel) or whether it is too large or too high-throughput for one node and needs sharding (Cluster).
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, Redis Sentinel is like a small branch with one head cashier and a couple of standby cashiers, plus a team of supervisors watching. If the head cashier faints, a quorum of supervisors agree and immediately promote a standby to head cashier — the branch keeps running, but it is still one branch holding one set of ledgers that fits in one room. Redis Cluster is like a whole network of branches where the bank splits all account numbers into sixteen thousand buckets and assigns each range of buckets to a different branch, each with its own standby staff. Now the data and the customers are spread across many branches, so no single branch is overwhelmed, and if one branch's head cashier faints, that branch's standby takes over while the others keep serving their own buckets. The first thing you ask is: how much data and how many customers? That decides whether you need one resilient branch or a sharded network.
s1_definition.oneliner: Choose Redis Sentinel when the data fits on one node and you only need automatic master failover by quorum, and choose Redis Cluster when the data or the request rate exceeds one node and you need horizontal sharding across 16384 hash slots, which is why the first question is always what kind and how much data lives in Redis.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Redis Sentinel and Redis Cluster solve two different problems. Sentinel provides high availability for a single logical dataset that fits on one node: a set of Sentinel processes monitor one master and its replicas, and when a quorum of Sentinels agrees the master is down, they promote a replica and update clients, giving automatic failover without sharding. Redis Cluster provides horizontal scaling and high availability together by partitioning the keyspace across 16384 hash slots, assigning ranges of slots to multiple masters (each with its own replicas), and routing every key to its slot with the formula CRC16 of the key modulo 16384, so the data and the request load spread across many nodes. The reason the first question is always "what kind of data is in Redis?" is that the answer tells you whether the dataset fits on one node and needs only failover (Sentinel) or whether it is too large or too high-throughput for one node and needs sharding (Cluster).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, Redis Sentinel is like a small branch with one head cashier and a couple of standby cashiers, plus a team of supervisors watching. If the head cashier faints, a quorum of supervisors agree and immediately promote a standby to head cashier — the branch keeps running, but it is still one branch holding one set of ledgers that fits in one room. Redis Cluster is like a whole network of branches where the bank splits all account numbers into sixteen thousand buckets and assigns each range of buckets to a different branch, each with its own standby staff. Now the data and the customers are spread across many branches, so no single branch is overwhelmed, and if one branch's head cashier faints, that branch's standby takes over while the others keep serving their own buckets. The first thing you ask is: how much data and how many customers? That decides whether you need one resilient branch or a sharded network.

**One line to remember:** Choose Redis Sentinel when the data fits on one node and you only need automatic master failover by quorum, and choose Redis Cluster when the data or the request rate exceeds one node and you need horizontal sharding across 16384 hash slots, which is why the first question is always what kind and how much data lives in Redis.

sections.s2_technical:
Redis Sentinel is a high-availability layer, not a sharding layer. You run one master Redis holding the entire dataset, one or more replicas that copy the master's data, and a separate set of Sentinel processes (an odd number, typically three or five, placed on independent hosts) whose only job is to watch. Each Sentinel pings the master, and if it stops responding, that Sentinel marks it subjectively down. Failover only happens when a quorum of Sentinels agree the master is objectively down, which prevents one flaky network link from triggering a needless failover. The Sentinels then elect a leader among themselves, choose the best replica (most up to date), promote it to master with the `REPLICAOF NO ONE` command, reconfigure the other replicas to follow the new master, and publish the new topology so clients reconnect to the right node. Clients use a Sentinel-aware library that asks the Sentinels "who is the current master?" rather than hardcoding an address.

The critical limitation of Sentinel is that the whole dataset must fit on a single node, because there is no sharding — every key lives on the one master, and the replicas are full copies for redundancy and read scaling, not partitions. So Sentinel scales reads (you can read from replicas) and gives you automatic failover, but it does not scale writes or memory beyond one machine. This makes Sentinel ideal for lightweight, bounded data: user sessions, one-time passwords, authentication tokens, feature flags, rate-limit counters — data that is individually small, collectively fits comfortably in one node's memory, and mainly needs to survive a node failure. For example a session store for ten million users at a kilobyte each is about ten gigabytes, which fits one node, so Sentinel is the right tool.

Redis Cluster is a sharding and high-availability layer combined. It divides the keyspace into exactly 16384 hash slots, and every key is mapped to a slot by taking the CRC16 hash of the key and taking it modulo 16384. For example the key `session:SAV2001` is routed by computing `CRC16("session:SAV2001") % 16384`, which yields a fixed slot number, and whichever master currently owns that slot stores the key. Slots are distributed across the master nodes — with three masters you might give slots 0 to 5460 to the first, 5461 to 10922 to the second, and 10923 to 16383 to the third — and each master has one or more replicas that take over if it fails. Because the data is partitioned, both memory and write throughput scale with the number of masters, which is the whole point.

Cluster clients are cluster-aware: they learn the slot-to-node map and send each command directly to the node owning that key's slot. If a client sends a command to the wrong node, the node replies with a MOVED or ASK redirection telling the client the correct node, and the client updates its map. A consequence of sharding is that multi-key operations only work when all the keys live in the same slot, which is why Redis Cluster supports hash tags: a key written as `{SAV2001}:balance` and `{SAV2001}:limit` forces both into the same slot because only the part inside the braces is hashed, so you can run a transaction or a multi-key command across them. Without hash tags, a multi-key command spanning different slots is rejected. This is a real design constraint you must plan keys around.

Failover in Cluster is per shard. If a master dies, its replicas and the other masters detect it via a gossip protocol, and the remaining masters vote to promote one of the dead master's replicas, so only that shard briefly fails over while the rest of the cluster keeps serving. Cluster needs at least three masters to form a healthy voting majority, and typically each master has at least one replica, so a minimum production cluster is six nodes. There is no separate Sentinel process in Cluster mode — the nodes monitor each other.

So the decision comes down to data characteristics, which is why the first question is "what kind of data is in Redis, and how much of it?" If the dataset is lightweight and fits comfortably on one node, and you mainly need automatic failover, Sentinel is simpler, cheaper, and fully sufficient — adding Cluster's complexity would be over-engineering. If the dataset is large (hundreds of gigabytes or more) or the write throughput exceeds what one node can handle, you have no choice but to shard, and Cluster is the answer, accepting its constraints around multi-key operations and the need for cluster-aware clients. A senior nuance is that managed offerings blur this: for example a managed Redis can run in a non-clustered mode with automatic failover (Sentinel-like) or a clustered mode, and the same decision logic applies. Another nuance is that you should not reach for Cluster merely for high availability — Sentinel already provides that — you reach for Cluster when you need horizontal scale, and the high availability comes along with it.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs two very different Redis workloads and must choose the right topology for each.

Problem 1 — The authentication team stores login sessions and one-time passwords. This data is small per item, expires quickly, and collectively fits in a few gigabytes, but it absolutely must survive a node crash because a failover that drops sessions would log every customer out. This is the Sentinel case: single node fits, needs automatic quorum failover.

Problem 2 — The pricing team caches market data and computed account dashboards for tens of millions of accounts, hundreds of gigabytes, at very high read and write rates that no single node can hold or serve. This is the Cluster case: too big and too hot for one node, needs sharding across hash slots.

Problem 3 — The pricing team needs to read an account's balance and credit limit together in one atomic multi-key operation, which in a sharded cluster only works if both keys land in the same slot. This is the hash-tag requirement.

We will model a topology advisor that, given a workload's data size and throughput, recommends Sentinel or Cluster, a slot router that computes a key's slot with a CRC16-modulo-16384 scheme and demonstrates hash tags forcing related keys into one slot, and a demo that routes session keys under Sentinel and dashboard keys under Cluster.

The code will have a `Workload` descriptor, a `TopologyAdvisor` that decides Sentinel versus Cluster, a `SlotRouter` implementing the slot formula and hash-tag extraction, and a demo that prints the recommendation for each workload and the slot assignments for several keys.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
javac RedisTopologyDemo.java
java RedisTopologyDemo

# Decision rule:
#   fits one node + just need failover → Sentinel (3 or 5 sentinels, quorum)
#   too big OR too hot for one node     → Cluster (≥3 masters, each with a replica = 6 nodes)
# Cluster key routing: slot = CRC16(key) % 16384 ; hash tags {acct} co-locate keys.
# Real setup:
#   redis-sentinel sentinel.conf           # Sentinel HA for sessions/OTPs/tokens
#   redis-cli --cluster create n1..n6 --cluster-replicas 1   # Cluster for big caches
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two workloads — an 8-gigabyte 40,000-QPS session-and-OTP store, and a 400-gigabyte 500,000-QPS dashboard cache — plus several keys to route.

Step 1 — The advisor evaluates the session store. Its 8 gigabytes is well under the 64-gigabyte single-node limit and its 40,000 QPS is under the 100,000 limit, so it fits one node and only needs failover. The advisor recommends Sentinel with quorum failover.

Step 2 — The advisor evaluates the dashboard cache. Its 400 gigabytes exceeds the single-node limit and its 500,000 QPS far exceeds the single-node QPS, so it cannot live on one node. The advisor recommends Cluster, sharding across the 16384 slots.

Step 3 — The slot router computes slots for several keys using CRC16 of the key modulo 16384. Each key deterministically maps to one fixed slot, and whichever master owns that slot stores the key. The data here is just the key string; the formula turns it into a slot number.

Step 4 — The demo shows that two unrelated dashboard keys for different accounts land in different slots, which is fine for single-key operations but means a multi-key command across them would be rejected because they live on potentially different masters.

Step 5 — The demo then shows hash tags: the keys with braces around the account id hash only the braced part, so both the balance key and the limit key for the same account produce the identical slot, which lets a multi-key operation or a transaction span them. This is how the pricing team reads balance and limit together atomically in a sharded cluster.

```
2026-10-24 17:18:05 [INFO] auth-sessions → SENTINEL (fits one node; quorum failover; lightweight sessions+otp)
2026-10-24 17:18:05 [INFO] pricing-cache → CLUSTER (shard across 16384 slots; data > one node & QPS > one node)
2026-10-24 17:18:05 [INFO] === Cluster slot routing (CRC16(key) % 16384) ===
2026-10-24 17:18:05 [INFO] key=session:SAV2001 → slot 10439
2026-10-24 17:18:05 [INFO] key=dashboard:CUR3001 → slot 4521
2026-10-24 17:18:05 [INFO] key=dashboard:SAV2001 → slot 866
2026-10-24 17:18:05 [INFO] === Hash tags keep an account's keys in one slot ===
2026-10-24 17:18:05 [INFO] {SAV2001}:balance → slot 2267 ; {SAV2001}:limit → slot 2267  SAME slot → multi-key op allowed
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Redis Sentinel and Redis Cluster solve two different problems, so the first question I always ask is what kind of data is in Redis and how much of it, because that answer decides between them. Sentinel is a high-availability layer for a dataset that fits on a single node — you run one master holding the whole dataset, some replicas, and a separate set of Sentinel processes that watch the master, and when a quorum of them agrees the master is down they elect a leader, promote the best replica, reconfigure the others, and publish the new topology so clients reconnect. It gives automatic failover and read scaling, but because there is no sharding it does not scale writes or memory beyond one machine.

That makes Sentinel ideal for lightweight, bounded data: sessions, one-time passwords, authentication tokens, feature flags, rate-limit counters — data that is individually small, collectively fits comfortably in one node, and mainly needs to survive a node failure without logging every customer out. For something like a session store of a few gigabytes, Sentinel is the right, simpler, cheaper choice, and reaching for Cluster there would be over-engineering.

Redis Cluster combines sharding and high availability. It divides the keyspace into exactly sixteen thousand three hundred eighty-four hash slots and maps every key to a slot with CRC16 of the key modulo sixteen thousand three hundred eighty-four, then spreads ranges of slots across multiple masters, each with its own replicas. Because the data is partitioned, both memory and write throughput scale with the number of masters. Clients are cluster-aware and learn the slot-to-node map, and if they hit the wrong node they get a MOVED or ASK redirection and update their map. The one real constraint is that multi-key operations only work when the keys share a slot, which is why you use hash tags — wrapping a common part of the key in braces so only that part is hashed — to force an account's related keys into the same slot.

In my banking work I used both. The authentication team's sessions and one-time passwords were a few gigabytes needing only resilient failover, so that ran on Sentinel with three sentinels and a quorum. The pricing team's dashboard and market-data cache was hundreds of gigabytes at very high throughput that no single node could hold or serve, so that ran on Redis Cluster, and I used hash tags around the account id so that balance and limit for the same account landed in one slot and could be read together atomically.

The framing I end on is that you do not pick Cluster merely for high availability, because Sentinel already provides that — you pick Cluster when you need horizontal scale because the data or the request rate exceeds a single node, and the high availability comes along for free. So the decision is genuinely driven by the data: fits one node and needs failover means Sentinel, exceeds one node and needs sharding means Cluster.
